examples.translation_ko: 내가 들은 바로는 그녀가 격렬한 감정의 소유자라는 것을 알고 있었다. 그리고 그토록 헌신적으로 자신을 사랑했던 남자 더크에게 가한 그 해로운 타격은 갑작스러운 성질과 끔찍한 잔혹함을 드러내는 것이었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English huswyfery, huswyffrye, howswyfry, equivalent to housewife + -ry.
definition_en: The management and maintenance of a household.

senses.gloss: The state or activity of being a housewife; household management, domestic skills.
senses.example: […] drafted by circumstance at too soon an age into a pinch-penny housewifery which might have existed just as well upon a lighthouse rock […]

senses.gloss: Synonym of household goods.
senses.example: Holonym: householdry

examples.text: It showed an eagerness for adventure, a readiness for the hand-to-mouth, which the care she took of her home and her love of good housewifery made not a little remarkable.
examples.translation_ko: 이는 모험에 대한 열망과 그날그날 살아가는 삶에 대한 각오를 보여주는 것이었는데, 집안을 돌보는 그녀의 세심함과 살림에 대한 애정을 생각하면 적지 않게 놀라운 일이었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Inherited from Middle English demure, demwre, an abbreviation of Anglo-Norman de mure port (“with a mature demeanor”) (compare Old French meur from...
definition_en: A woman who is modest and reserved in her behavior.

senses.gloss: Modest, quiet, reserved, or serious.
senses.example: She is a demure young lady.

senses.gloss: Affectedly modest, decorous, or serious; making a show of gravity.
senses.example: Miss Lizzy, I have no doubt, would be as demure and coquettish, as if ten winters more had gone over her head.

examples.text: She must be a woman of complicated character, and there was something dramatic in the contrast of that with her demure appearance.
examples.translation_ko: 그녀는 분명 복잡한 성격의 소유자였고, 그런 면과 그녀의 얌전한 외모 사이의 대조에는 뭔가 극적인 것이 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English busily, busiliche, bisili, bisiliche, equivalent to busy + -ly.
definition_en: Working diligently and energetically.

senses.gloss: In a busy manner; actively.
senses.example: Quite a crowd of townspeople turned out to see the train start, and several pressmen were busily engaged in taking notes and photographs.

examples.text: I was excited by the encounter, and my fancy worked busily while I sought to concentrate myself on the game I was playing.
examples.translation_ko: 나는 그 만남에 흥분했고, 게임에 집중하려고 애쓰는 동안 상상력이 분주하게 돌아갔다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Borrowed from Latin oppōnēns (“opposing”), present active participle of oppōnō (“I oppose”).
definition_en: A person or team that is competing against another.

senses.gloss: One who opposes another physically (in a fight, sport, game, or competition).
senses.example: […] it is possible for a good [draughts] player to defeat an opponent without capturing his pieces.

senses.gloss: One who opposes another in words (in a dispute, argument or controversy).
senses.example: “What more have you to say?” she asked, rather in the tone in which a person might address an opponent of adult age than such as is ordinarily used to a child.

senses.gloss: One who is opposed or objects (to a policy, course of action or set of ideas).
senses.example: She was a dedicated opponent of the death penalty.

examples.text: I always tried my best to beat Strickland, because he was a player who despised the opponent he vanquished; his exultation in victory made defeat more difficult to bear.
examples.translation_ko: 나는 항상 스트릭랜드를 이기려고 최선을 다했는데, 그는 자신이 이긴 상대를 경멸하는 선수였기 때문이다. 승리에 대한 그의 득의양양함은 패배를 더욱 견디기 어렵게 만들었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English venquysshen, vaynquisshen, borrowed from a conjugated form of Old French veincre, from Latin vincō.
definition_en: Defeat or overcome a person or thing.

senses.gloss: To defeat (someone); to overcome.
senses.example: They […] vanquished the rebels in all encounters.

examples.text: I always tried my best to beat Strickland, because he was a player who despised the opponent he vanquished; his exultation in victory made defeat more difficult to bear.
examples.translation_ko: 나는 항상 스트릭랜드를 이기려고 최선을 다했는데, 그는 자신이 이긴 상대를 경멸하는 선수였기 때문이다. 승리에 대한 그의 득의양양함은 패배를 더욱 견디기 어렵게 만들었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English victory, victori, victorie (“supremacy, victory; a defeat or vanquishing, conquest; superior military force...
definition_en: The state of having won a contest or achieved a goal.

senses.gloss: The condition or state of having won a battle or competition, or having succeeded in an effort; (countable) an instance of this.
senses.example: It was a great victory on the battlefield.

senses.gloss: Alternative letter-case form of Victory (“(uncountable) the Roman goddess of victory, the counterpart of the Greek goddess Nike; also (countable), an artistic depiction of her, chiefly as a winged woman”).

examples.text: I always tried my best to beat Strickland, because he was a player who despised the opponent he vanquished; his exultation in victory made defeat more difficult to bear.
examples.translation_ko: 나는 항상 스트릭랜드를 이기려고 최선을 다했는데, 그는 자신이 이긴 상대를 경멸하는 선수였기 때문이다. 승리에 대한 그의 득의양양함은 패배를 더욱 견디기 어렵게 만들었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English defeten, from Middle English defet (“disfigured”, past participle) and defet (“defect”, noun), see Etymology 2 below.
definition_en: A loss or defeat in a contest or struggle.

senses.gloss: To overcome in battle or contest.
senses.example: Wellington defeated Napoleon at Waterloo.

senses.gloss: To reduce, to nothing, the strength of.
senses.example: In one instance he defeated his own purpose.

senses.gloss: To nullify
senses.example: The escheators […] defeated the right heir of his succession.

examples.text: I always tried my best to beat Strickland, because he was a player who despised the opponent he vanquished; his exultation in victory made defeat more difficult to bear.
examples.translation_ko: 나는 항상 스트릭랜드를 이기려고 최선을 다했는데, 그는 자신이 이긴 상대를 경멸하는 선수였기 때문이다. 승리에 대한 그의 득의양양함은 패배를 더욱 견디기 어렵게 만들었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Inherited from Middle English wynner, wynnere, equivalent to win + -er. Compare Saterland Frisian Winner (“winner”), West Frisian winner (“winner”)...
definition_en: A person or team that wins a competition.

senses.gloss: One who has won or often wins.
A point or goal that wins a competition.
senses.example: It was a fitting scoreline on the club's landmark anniversary, and appropriate that Van Persie should get the winner.

examples.text: He was a bad winner and a good loser.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 이길 때는 못된 승자였고 질 때는 좋은 패자였다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English loser, losere, equivalent to lose + -er. In the sense of contemptible or worthless individual, perhaps an alteration of losel, ...
definition_en: A person who has failed or is unsuccessful.

senses.gloss: A person who loses; one who fails to win or thrive.
senses.example: In a two-horse race there is always one winner and one loser.

senses.gloss: Something of poor quality.
A person who is frequently unsuccessful in life.
senses.example: That guy is a born loser!

examples.text: He was a bad winner and a good loser.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 이길 때는 못된 승자였고 질 때는 좋은 패자였다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From un- + warranted.
definition_en: Not justified or supported.

senses.gloss: Not warranted; being without warrant, authority, or guaranty; unwarrantable.
Unjustified, inappropriate or undeserved.
senses.example: This strike action by the RMT is completely unwarranted and unjustified.

examples.text: No word had been said to give me anything to think about, and any surmises I might make were unwarranted.
examples.translation_ko: 내가 생각해볼 만한 것을 줄 수 있는 말은 한 마디도 나오지 않았고, 내가 할 수 있는 어떤 추측도 근거가 없는 것이었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Borrowed from French intrigue, from Italian intricare, from Latin intrīcō (“I entangle, perplex, embarrass”). Doublet of intricate.
definition_en: To secretly plot or scheme against someone.

senses.gloss: A complicated or clandestine plot or scheme intended to effect some purpose by secret artifice; conspiracy; stratagem.
senses.example: […] lost in such a jungle of intrigues, pettifoggings, treacheries, diplomacies domestic and foreign […]

senses.gloss: The plot of a play, poem or romance; the series of complications in which a writer involves their imaginary characters.
Clandestine intercourse between persons; illicit intimacy; a liaison or affair.
senses.example: In 1679 and 1680 there were persistent rumors of an intrigue between Mary, Lady Grey, and the Duke of Monmouth.

examples.text: I was intrigued.
examples.translation_ko: 나는 호기심이 생겼다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From un- + changed.
definition_en: Remaining the same.

senses.gloss: Not changed or altered; remaining in an original state.

examples.text: “Absolutely unchanged.”
examples.translation_ko: "전혀 변하지 않았어요."
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From emotional + -ly.
definition_en: Relating to or characterized by emotions.

senses.gloss: In an emotional manner; displaying emotion.
Regarding emotions.
senses.example: Physically, it was easy, but emotionally it was the hardest thing I've ever done.

examples.text: He clasped his hands emotionally.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 감정에 북받쳐 두 손을 꼭 쥐었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From excite + -able.
definition_en: Having or showing a tendency to be easily excited.

senses.gloss: Easily excited.
senses.example: The excitable puppy jumped all over the furniture.

senses.gloss: Able to respond to external stimuli.
Able to be promoted to an excited state.

examples.text: Stroeve had always been excitable, but now he was beside himself; there was no reasoning with him.
examples.translation_ko: 스트루브는 원래 흥분을 잘 하는 성격이었지만, 지금은 완전히 제정신이 아니었다. 그와는 이성적인 대화가 불가능했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition_en: The process of thinking about or discussing the reasons for something.

senses.gloss: The deduction of inferences or interpretations from premises, abstract thought, ratiocination; (countable) any instance of this, especially as a process leading to an action, motive.
A Rastafari meeting held for the purposes of chanting, prayer and discussion.

examples.text: Stroeve had always been excitable, but now he was beside himself; there was no reasoning with him.
examples.translation_ko: 스트루브는 원래 흥분을 잘 하는 성격이었지만, 지금은 완전히 제정신이 아니었다. 그와는 이성적인 대화가 불가능했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Borrowed from Middle French tolerable, from Latin tolerābilis.
definition_en: Acceptable but not good.

senses.gloss: Capable of being borne, tolerated or endured; bearable or endurable.
Moderate in degree; mediocre; passable, acceptable or so-so.
senses.example: A cabled despatch is better than nothing, but a voicecast of tolerable quality is preferable, and in certain types of story a voicecast with live or recorded actuality is best of all.

senses.gloss: Such as to be tolerated or countenanced; permissible; allowable.

examples.text: I thought it probable enough that Blanche Stroeve would not continue to find life with Strickland tolerable, but one of the falsest of proverbs is that you must lie on the bed that you have made.
examples.translation_ko: 블랑슈 스트루브가 스트릭랜드와의 생활을 계속 견딜 수 있으리라고는 생각하지 않았지만, '자신이 깐 자리에는 자신이 누워야 한다'는 속담만큼 거짓된 것도 없다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Old French proverbe, from Latin proverbium.
definition_en: A short saying that expresses a general truth or piece of advice.

senses.gloss: A commonly used sentence expressing popular wisdom.
senses.example: Near-synonyms: aphorism, maxim, adage, saw, saying, apothegm, byword, paroemia, sententia (Latin)

senses.gloss: Any commonly used turn of phrase expressing a metaphor, simile, or descriptive epithet.
A striking or paradoxical assertion; an obscure saying; an enigma; a parable.
senses.example: His disciples said unto him, Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb.

examples.text: I thought it probable enough that Blanche Stroeve would not continue to find life with Strickland tolerable, but one of the falsest of proverbs is that you must lie on the bed that you have made.
examples.translation_ko: 블랑슈 스트루브가 스트릭랜드와의 생활을 계속 견딜 수 있으리라고는 생각하지 않았지만, '자신이 깐 자리에는 자신이 누워야 한다'는 속담만큼 거짓된 것도 없다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle French évader, from Latin ēvādō (“I pass or go over; flee”), from ē (“out of, from”) + vādō (“I go; walk”). See also wade.
definition_en: Avoid or escape something.

senses.gloss: To get away from by cunning; to avoid by using dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to cleverly escape from
senses.example: He evaded his opponent's blows.

senses.gloss: To escape; to slip away; — sometimes with from.
senses.example: Unarmed they might / Have easily, as spirits evaded swift / By quick contraction or remove.

senses.gloss: To attempt to escape; to practice artifice or sophistry, for the purpose of eluding.
senses.example: The ministers of God are not to evade and take refuge any of these ... ways.

examples.text: The experience of life shows that people are constantly doing things which must lead to disaster, and yet by some chance manage to evade the result of their folly.
examples.translation_ko: 인생 경험을 보면 사람들은 끊임없이 재앙으로 이어질 수밖에 없는 일들을 저지르면서도, 어떤 우연한 기회로 자신의 어리석음이 초래할 결과를 피해 나간다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English humbely, humbliche, equivalent to humble + -ly. Displaced Old English ēaþmōdlīċe.
definition_en: Used to express modesty or humility.

senses.gloss: In a humble manner.
senses.example: I humbly accept this award.

examples.text: When Blanche quarrelled with Strickland she had only to leave him, and her husband was waiting humbly to forgive and forget.
examples.translation_ko: 블랑슈가 스트릭랜드와 다투면 그냥 그를 떠나기만 하면 되었고, 남편은 겸손하게 용서하고 잊어주기를 기다리고 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English woful, waful, equivalent to woe + -ful. Compare Old English wālīċ (“woeful”), Old English tēonful (“woeful”).
definition_en: Causing or expressing sadness or sorrow.

senses.gloss: Full of woe; sorrowful; distressed with grief or calamity.
senses.example: How many woeful widows left to bow / To sad disgrace!

senses.gloss: Bringing calamity, distress, or affliction.
senses.example: a woeful event

senses.gloss: Lamentable, deplorable.
senses.example:
Thou seest we are not all alone unhappy:
This wide and universal theatre
Presents more woeful pageants than the scene
Wherein we play in.

examples.text: Stroeve gave me a look with his woeful eyes.
examples.translation_ko: 스트루브가 슬픈 눈으로 나를 바라보았다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From intense + -ly.
definition_en: Feeling or showing a strong and intense degree of something.

senses.gloss: In an intense manner.
senses.example: He pursued his studies intensely.

senses.gloss: To an intense degree, extremely.
senses.example: An intensely private man, he kept chit-chat to a minimum.

examples.text: “Of course it doesn’t much matter to you, but to me it’s so serious, so intensely serious.”
examples.translation_ko: "물론 당신에게는 별로 중요하지 않겠지만, 저에게는 너무나 심각한, 정말 극도로 심각한 문제예요."
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: 1595, from Northern English dialectal flippand (“prattling, babbling, glib”), present participle of flip (“to babble”), of North Germanic origin. C...
definition_en: Showing a lack of respect or seriousness.

senses.gloss: Showing disrespect through a casual attitude, levity, and a lack of due seriousness; pert.
senses.example: Our society treats smoking flippantly as a slightly distasteful habit that can injure your health. It is not. It is drug addiction.

senses.gloss: Loquacious; speaking with ease and rapidity.
senses.example:
November 5, 1673, Isaac Barrow, sermon on the Gunpowder Treason
It becometh good men, in such cases, to be pleasantly flippant and free in their speech.

senses.gloss: Nimble; limber.

examples.text: I was sorry if I had seemed impatient or flippant.
examples.translation_ko: 내가 성급하거나 경솔하게 보였다면 미안했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From hand + writing, equal to handwrite + -ing.
definition_en: The style or quality of writing that a person uses.

senses.gloss: The act or process of writing done with the hand, rather than typed or word-processed.
Text that was written by hand.
The characteristic writing of a particular person.
senses.example: Great libraries are only just beginning to gather up the manuscript minutiae which their books contain; to identify handwritings; to decipher monograms; to collect facts.

examples.text: He was conscious that she regarded him with an indifference so profound that the sight of his handwriting would have not the slightest effect on her.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 아내가 자신을 너무나 깊은 무관심으로 대하고 있어서, 자신의 필체를 보는 것조차 그녀에게 조금의 영향도 주지 못하리라는 것을 알고 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From un- + altered.
definition_en: Not changed or modified.

senses.gloss: Remaining in its initial state; not changed.
senses.example: But beyond these cut-offs, to avoid the wholesale alteration of all mileposting and mileages—of bridges and culverts, for example—the original mileposts have remained unaltered.

examples.text: His love for you is unaltered.
examples.translation_ko: 당신에 대한 그의 사랑은 변하지 않았다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From disastrous + -ly.
definition_en: Causing or resulting from a disaster.

senses.gloss: In a disastrous way. (Of the nature of a disaster; calamitously.)
senses.example: Mr. Dukakis charged that when it came to advising President Reagan on Iran, Mr. Bush was "disastrously and completely and unforgivably wrong."

examples.text: But though I was no less convinced than Stroeve that the connection between Strickland and Blanche would end disastrously, I did not expect the issue to take the tragic form it did.
examples.translation_ko: 하지만 스트릭랜드와 블랑슈의 관계가 파멸적으로 끝날 것이라고 스트루브만큼이나 확신했음에도 불구하고, 나는 그 결말이 실제로 일어난 것처럼 비극적인 형태를 띨 것이라고는 예상하지 못했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From sulter (“verb (obsolete), a variant of swelter”) + -y; compare sweltry.
definition_en: A warm and humid atmosphere.

senses.gloss: Hot and humid; sweltering.
senses.example: The heat had been painfully oppressive all day; and it was now a close and sultry night.

senses.gloss: Emitting great heat.
senses.example: The battlefield—an undulating, parched, and dusty expanse—is lying under the sultry sun of a July afternoon.

senses.gloss: Sexually enthralling.

examples.text: The summer came, breathless and sultry, and even at night there was no coolness to rest one’s jaded nerves.
examples.translation_ko: 여름이 왔다. 숨막히고 무더운 여름이었고, 밤이 되어도 지친 신경을 달래줄 서늘함은 찾아볼 수 없었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Borrowed from French le jade, rebracketing of earlier l'éjade (“jade”), from Spanish piedra de ijada (“flank stone”), via Vulgar Latin *iliata from...
definition_en: To feel a sense of calm or serenity.

senses.gloss: A semiprecious stone, either nephrite or jadeite, generally green or white in color, often used for carving figurines.
A bright shade of slightly bluish or greyish green, typical of polished jade stones.
A succulent plant, Crassula ovata.

examples.text: The summer came, breathless and sultry, and even at night there was no coolness to rest one’s jaded nerves.
examples.translation_ko: 여름이 왔다. 숨막히고 무더운 여름이었고, 밤이 되어도 지친 신경을 달래줄 서늘함은 찾아볼 수 없었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English laiten, leiten, from Old Norse leita (“to seek, search, inquire”), from Proto-Germanic *wlaitōną (“to look out, see”), from Pro...
definition_en: A type of milk or a person who milks cows.

senses.gloss: To seek; search for; inquire.
senses.example: By neeght, o' my bed, I laited him, at my sowl luvs : I laited him, but I dudn't find um.

examples.text: By my side was the empty bowl in which the concierge had brought me my café au lait and the fragment of croissant which I had not had appetite enough to eat.
examples.translation_ko: 내 곁에는 관리인이 가져다준 카페오레를 마신 빈 그릇과 식욕이 없어서 다 먹지 못한 크루아상 조각이 놓여 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French croissant (“crescent”), present participle of croître (“to grow”). Doublet of crescent.
definition_en: Flaky pastry

senses.gloss: A flaky roll or pastry in a form of a crescent.

examples.text: By my side was the empty bowl in which the concierge had brought me my café au lait and the fragment of croissant which I had not had appetite enough to eat.

definition_en: A person who is trained to give spiritual guidance and care to a local Christian community.

senses.gloss: Someone who tends to a flock of animals: synonym of shepherd.
Someone with spiritual authority over a group of people.
A minister or priest in a church.

examples.text: She showed my sketches to the pastor and the doctor and the judge.
examples.translation_ko: 어머니는 제 스케치를 목사님과 의사 선생님, 판사님께 보여드렸죠.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English winnen, from Old English winnan (“to labour, swink, toil,”) (compare Old English ġewinnan (“conquer, obtain, gain; endure, bear...
definition_en: To gain or achieve something successfully.

senses.gloss: To conquer, defeat.
senses.example: For the glory, the power to win the Black Lord, I will search for the Emerald Sword.

senses.gloss: To reach some destination or object, despite difficulty or toil (now usually intransitive, with preposition or locative adverb).
senses.example:
And when the stony path began,
 By which the naked peak they won,
 Up flew the snowy ptarmigan.

senses.gloss: To triumph or achieve victory in (a game, a war, etc.).

examples.text: And they sent me to Amsterdam to try for a scholarship, and I won it.
examples.translation_ko: 그래서 그분들이 저를 암스테르담으로 보내 장학금 시험을 치르게 했고, 제가 합격했어요.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English pinchen, from Old Northern French *pinchier (compare Old French pincier, pincer (“to pinch”)), a word of uncertain origin, poss...
definition_en: To grip or hold something tightly with the fingers.

senses.gloss: To squeeze a small amount of a person's skin and flesh, making it hurt.
senses.example: The children were scolded for pinching each other.

senses.gloss: To squeeze between the thumb and forefinger.
To squeeze between two objects.
senses.example: Since the resistance of the channel is inversely proportional to its width, the most resistive region is the one pinched between the gates where they come closest to each other.

examples.text: They pinched and saved so that I should have enough to live on, and when my first picture was exhibited they came to Amsterdam to see it, my father and mother and my sister, and my mother cried when she looked at it.”
examples.translation_ko: 가족들은 제가 생활할 수 있을 만큼 충분한 돈을 마련하려고 허리띠를 졸라매며 저축했고, 제 첫 작품이 전시되었을 때는 아버지와 어머니, 누이가 그것을 보러 암스테르담까지 오셨는데, 어머니는 그 그림을 보고 우셨어요."
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English olyve, from Old French olive (“olive, olive tree”), from Latin olīva (“olive”), itself either from Etruscan *𐌄𐌋𐌄𐌉𐌅𐌀 (*eleiva), ...
definition_en: A small green or black fruit that is often pickled and used as a condiment.

senses.gloss: A tree of species Olea europaea cultivated since ancient times in the Mediterranean for its fruit and the oil obtained from it.
The small oval fruit of this tree, eaten ripe (usually black) or unripe (usually green).
senses.example: Trevor, like an Aussie outbacker, eats snacks and a pickup meal of bread, cantaloupe, olives, mangoes, and melon.

senses.gloss: The wood of the olive tree.

examples.text: I thought of those cold scenes of his, with their picturesque peasants and cypresses and olive-trees.
examples.translation_ko: 나는 그림 같은 농부들과 사이프러스 나무, 올리브 나무가 있는 그의 차가운 풍경화들을 떠올렸다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Unknown, possibly from obsolete Middle English gawren (“to stare”) which is of uncertain origin, probably from Old Norse gá (“to watch, heed”) or g...
definition_en: Overly showy or tastelessly ornate.

senses.gloss: Overly ostentatious; so colorful as to be in bad taste.
senses.example: The dress fits her well, but the pattern is rather garish.

examples.text: They must look queer in their garish frames on the walls of the peasant house.
examples.translation_ko: 농가 벽에 걸린 화려한 액자 속에서 그 그림들은 분명 어색해 보일 것이다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English prevailen, from Old French prevaler, from Latin praevaleō (“be very able or more able, be superior, prevail”), from prae (“befo...
definition_en: To succeed or be effective.

senses.gloss: To be superior in strength, dominance, influence, or frequency; to have or gain the advantage over others; to have the upper hand; to outnumber others.
senses.example: Red colour prevails in the Canadian flag.

senses.gloss: To triumph; to be victorious.
senses.example: There are a number of SCPs and tales that look at potential apocalypses, but rarely with such totality as SCP-2935, a parallel dimension in which death prevailed.

senses.gloss: To be current, widespread, or predominant; to have currency or prevalence.
senses.example: In his day and age, such practices prevailed all over Europe.

examples.text: “The dear soul thought she was doing a wonderful thing for me when she made me an artist, but perhaps, after all, it would have been better for me if my father’s will had prevailed and I were now but an honest carpenter.”
examples.translation_ko: "그 착한 분은 나를 화가로 만들어주는 것이 나에게 놀라운 일을 해주는 것이라고 생각했지만, 어쩌면 결국 아버지의 뜻대로 지금 정직한 목수가 되어 있었다면 나에게 더 좋았을지도 모르겠어요."
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English impellen, borrowed from Latin impellō.
definition_en: To urge or force someone to do something.

senses.gloss: To urge a person; to press on; to incite to action or motion via intrinsic motivation.
senses.example: Concern for the common good should impel us to find ways to overcome the devilish impact of these disastrous policies […]

senses.gloss: To drive forward; to propel an object, to provide an impetus for motion or action.
senses.example: The wind impelled the kayaks toward the shore.

examples.text: Something impelled him to go to the studio, some obscure desire for self-torture, and yet he dreaded the anguish that he foresaw.
examples.translation_ko: 무언가가 그를 화실로 향하게 했다. 자기 자신을 괴롭히려는 어떤 막연한 욕망이었지만, 동시에 그는 예상되는 고통을 두려워했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Formed from ascend on the model of descend/descent.
definition_en: The act of rising or climbing to a higher position.

senses.gloss: The act of ascending; a motion upwards.
senses.example: He made a tedious ascent of Mont Blanc.

senses.gloss: The way or means by which one ascends.
senses.example: There is a difficult northern ascent from Malaucene of Mont Ventoux.

senses.gloss: An eminence, hill, or high place.

examples.text: He remembered how often he had waited for a minute or two on the landing to get his breath after the ascent, and how absurdly his impatience to see Blanche had taken it away again.
examples.translation_ko: 계단을 오르고 나서 숨을 고르기 위해 층계참에서 1, 2분 기다리곤 했던 일들이 떠올랐고, 블랑슈를 보고 싶은 조급함이 그 숨을 다시 가쁘게 만들었던 것도 우스울 정도였다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From absurd + -ly.
definition_en: Used to describe something as extremely foolish or unreasonable.

senses.gloss: In an absurd fashion.
senses.example: He orated absurdly.

senses.gloss: To an extreme degree.
senses.example: The critics were absurdly extravagant with their praise.

examples.text: He remembered how often he had waited for a minute or two on the landing to get his breath after the ascent, and how absurdly his impatience to see Blanche had taken it away again.
examples.translation_ko: 계단을 오르고 나서 숨을 고르기 위해 층계참에서 1, 2분 기다리곤 했던 일들이 떠올랐고, 블랑슈를 보고 싶은 조급함이 그 숨을 다시 가쁘게 만들었던 것도 우스울 정도였다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Latin exquīsītus (“to be outsought”), perfect passive participle of exquīrō (“I outseek”).
definition_en: Extremely beautiful or delicate.

senses.gloss: Specially fine or pleasing; exceptional.
senses.example: They sell good coffee and pastries, but their chocolate is exquisite.

senses.gloss: Carefully adjusted; precise; accurate; exact.
Recherché; far-fetched; abstruse.

examples.text: What had happened could only be a dream, a frightful dream; and when he turned the key and opened the door, he would see her bending slightly over the table in the gracious attitude of the woman in Chardin’s Benedicite, which always seemed to him so exquisite.
examples.translation_ko: 일어난 일은 꿈, 끔찍한 꿈일 뿐이었다. 열쇠를 돌려 문을 열면 샤르댕의 「식사 기도」 속 여인의 우아한 자세로 테이블 위에 살짝 몸을 굽히고 있는 그녀를 보게 될 것이었다. 그 자세는 언제나 그에게 너무도 아름다워 보였다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Borrowed from Middle French désertion.
definition_en: The act of leaving a place or position without permission.

senses.gloss: The act of deserting.

examples.text: The apartment had no look of desertion.
examples.translation_ko: 아파트에는 버려진 기색이 전혀 없었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From tidy + -ness.
definition_en: The state of being tidy or well-organized.

senses.gloss: The quality of being tidy.

examples.text: His wife’s tidiness was one of the traits which had so much pleased him; his own upbringing had given him a tender sympathy for the delight in orderliness; and when he had seen her instinctive desire to put each thing in its appointed place it had given him a little warm feeling in his heart.
examples.translation_ko: 아내의 정돈된 생활은 그를 그토록 기쁘게 했던 특징 중 하나였다. 그 자신의 성장 배경이 질서를 좋아하는 마음에 대한 따뜻한 공감을 심어주었고, 모든 것을 제자리에 두려는 그녀의 본능적인 욕구를 보았을 때 그의 마음에 작은 따뜻함을 안겨주었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English comb, from Old English camb (“comb”), from Proto-West Germanic *kamb, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz (“comb”), from Proto-Indo-Eur...
definition_en: A tool for untangling or arranging hair.

senses.gloss: A toothed implement for grooming the hair or (formerly) for keeping it in place.
A machine used in separating choice cotton fibers from worsted cloth fibers.
The toothed plate at the top and bottom of an escalator that prevents objects getting trapped between the moving stairs and fixed landings.

examples.text: The bedroom looked as though she had just left it: the brushes were neatly placed on the toilet-table, one on each side of the comb; someone had smoothed down the bed on which she had spent her last night in the studio; and her nightdress in a little case lay on the pillow.
examples.translation_ko: 침실은 그녀가 방금 나간 것처럼 보였다. 빗들은 화장대 위에 빗을 사이에 두고 양쪽에 하나씩 가지런히 놓여 있었고, 누군가 그녀가 작업실에서 보낸 마지막 밤을 지낸 침대를 매끄럽게 정리해 놓았으며, 작은 케이스에 든 잠옷이 베개 위에 놓여 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From night + dress.
definition_en: A loose-fitting nightgown or dressing gown.

senses.gloss: A nightgown; (usually female) attire designed to be worn to bed.
senses.example: She was too modest to come downstairs dressed only in her nightdress.

examples.text: The bedroom looked as though she had just left it: the brushes were neatly placed on the toilet-table, one on each side of the comb; someone had smoothed down the bed on which she had spent her last night in the studio; and her nightdress in a little case lay on the pillow.
examples.translation_ko: 침실은 그녀가 방금 나간 것처럼 보였다. 빗들은 화장대 위에 빗을 사이에 두고 양쪽에 하나씩 가지런히 놓여 있었고, 누군가 그녀가 작업실에서 보낸 마지막 밤을 지낸 침대를 매끄럽게 정리해 놓았으며, 작은 케이스에 든 잠옷이 베개 위에 놓여 있었다.

definition_en: A type of food made from milk.

senses.gloss: A dairy product made from curdled or cultured milk.
Any particular variety of cheese.
A piece of cheese, especially one moulded into a large round shape during manufacture.

examples.text: Under a cover were the remains of a piece of cheese, and in a tin box was a crust of bread.
examples.translation_ko: 덮개 아래에는 치즈 조각이 남아 있었고, 양철 상자 안에는 빵 껍질이 들어 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English cruste, from Anglo-Norman and Old French cruste, from Latin crusta (“hard outer covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (...
definition_en: The outer layer of the earth or a baked covering for food.

senses.gloss: A more solid, dense or hard layer on a surface or boundary.
The external, hardened layer of certain foodstuffs, including most types of bread, fried meat, etc.
An outer layer composed of pastry
senses.example: They […] made the crust for the venison pasty.

examples.text: Under a cover were the remains of a piece of cheese, and in a tin box was a crust of bread.
examples.translation_ko: 덮개 아래에는 치즈 조각이 남아 있었고, 양철 상자 안에는 빵 껍질이 들어 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From strict + -ly.
definition_en: Used to indicate that something is done or applied exactly according to rules.

senses.gloss: In a strict manner.
senses.example: He adhered strictly to the diet his doctor prescribed.

senses.gloss: In a limited manner; only
senses.example: This work was strictly voluntary, but any animal who absented himself from it would have his rations reduced by half.

senses.gloss: In a narrow or limited sense.
senses.example: That term refers strictly to smaller birds.

examples.text: She had done her marketing from day to day, buying only what was strictly needful, so that nothing was left over from one day to the next.
examples.translation_ko: 그녀는 날마다 장을 보면서 꼭 필요한 것만 사서, 하루에서 다음 날로 넘어가는 것이 아무것도 없도록 했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From methodical + -ness.
definition_en: The quality of being methodical.

senses.gloss: The property of being methodical.

examples.text: Her methodicalness made her suicide more deliberate.
examples.translation_ko: 그녀의 체계적인 성격이 자살을 더욱 의도적인 것으로 만들었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English spoon, spoune, spone, spon (“spoon, chip of wood”), from Old English spōn (“sliver, chip of wood, shaving”), from Proto-West Ge...
definition_en: A utensil used for eating or serving food.

senses.gloss: An implement for eating or serving; a scooped utensil whose long handle is straight, in contrast to a ladle.
senses.example: He must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil.

senses.gloss: An implement for stirring food while being prepared; a wooden spoon.
A measure that will fit into a spoon; a spoonful.
senses.example: While Ms. Fly was with Sharon in the kitchen, Sharon asked the defendant for a “spoon of drugs.” Defendant refused and stated that he did not know where drugs could be obtained.

examples.text: He had a sudden vision of her standing in the kitchen—it was hardly larger than a cupboard—washing the plates and glasses, the forks and spoons, giving the knives a rapid polish on the knife-board; and then putting everything away, giving the sink a scrub, and hanging the dish-cloth up to dry—it was there still, a gray torn rag; then looking round to see that everything was clean and nice.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 갑자기 그녀가 부엌에 서 있는 모습이 눈에 떠올랐다—찬장보다 조금 클 뿐인 그 부엌에서 접시와 잔들, 포크와 숟가락을 씻고, 칼판에 칼들을 재빠르게 닦아내고, 그런 다음 모든 것을 제자리에 정리하고, 개수대를 문지르고, 행주를 걸어 말리는—그 행주는 아직도 거기 있었다, 회색빛 너덜너덜한 걸레가—그리고 나서 모든 것이 깨끗하고 말끔한지 둘러보는 모습이.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Occitan brocada and Spanish and Portuguese brocado, influenced by French brocart, from Italian broccato, from brocco, ultimately from Gaulish.
definition_en: A richly ornamental fabric with intricate patterns.

senses.gloss: A thick heavy fabric into which raised patterns have been woven, originally in gold and silver; more recently any cloth incorporating raised, woven patterns.
senses.example: … his desire to stand in brocade and sing Rhadames in Aida was like my eagerness to go far, far beyond fellow intellectuals of my generation who had lost the imaginative soul.

senses.gloss: An item decorated with brocade.
Any of several species of noctuid moths such as some species in the genera Calophasia and Hadena
senses.example: Other species considered occasional migrants have become established in the UK in recent years, such as the ... sombre brocade, Blair's mocha, Flame brocade, and Clifden nonpareil.

examples.text: There were bits of old brocade on the walls, and the piano was covered with a piece of silk, beautiful and tarnished; in one corner was a copy of the Venus of Milo, and in another of the Venus of the Medici.
examples.translation_ko: 벽에는 낡은 비단 조각들이 걸려 있었고, 피아노는 아름답지만 빛바랜 비단으로 덮여 있었다. 한쪽 구석에는 밀로의 비너스 복제품이, 다른 구석에는 메디치의 비너스 복제품이 놓여 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English ternysshen, from Old French terniss-, stem of ternir (“to make dim, make wan”), borrowed from Old High German *ternen, tarnen, ...
definition_en: Become less shiny or bright.

senses.gloss: Oxidation or discoloration, especially of a decorative metal exposed to air.
senses.example: Limiting the use of silver to special occasions might invite tarnish unless the pieces are carefully protected.

examples.text: There were bits of old brocade on the walls, and the piano was covered with a piece of silk, beautiful and tarnished; in one corner was a copy of the Venus of Milo, and in another of the Venus of the Medici.
examples.translation_ko: 벽에는 낡은 비단 조각들이 걸려 있었고, 피아노는 아름답지만 빛바랜 비단으로 덮여 있었다. 한쪽 구석에는 밀로의 비너스 복제품이, 다른 구석에는 메디치의 비너스 복제품이 놓여 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English surmounten, from Old French surmonter (“to rise above, surmount”), from sur- (“above”) + monter (“to mount”), equivalent to sur...
definition_en: To overcome or dominate something.

senses.gloss: To get or be over without touching or resting on; to overcome.
senses.example: Burkina Fasoan legislation surmounts one more step which sees in the organ created in this country and designated as the Superior Council of Information (S.C.I.), " an administrative authority".

senses.gloss: To cap; to sit on top of.
senses.example: The ovolo surmounting the dentil course generally turns the corner by means of a carved acanthus leaf, the decorated cyma and cyma reversa being similarly treated at the corner.

examples.text: Here and there was an Italian cabinet surmounted with Delft, and here and there a bas-relief.
examples.translation_ko: 여기저기에는 델프트 도자기를 올린 이탈리아식 캐비닛이 있었고, 또 여기저기에는 부조가 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: First attested in Scottish English (compare Scots stob, stobbe, stabb (“a pointed stick or stake; a thrust with a pointed weapon”)), from Middle En...
definition_en: A wound caused by a sharp pointed object.

senses.gloss: An act of stabbing or thrusting with an object.
senses.example: A knife was flashing in his hand, and just as he was about to take a stab at me, the smith grabbed his arm from behind.

senses.gloss: A wound made by stabbing.
senses.example: I opened the man's linen robe, and there over his heart was a dagger-wound, and beneath the woman's fair breast was a like cruel stab, through which her life had ebbed away.

senses.gloss: Pain inflicted on a person's feelings.
senses.example: “I bet you two have really big plans. And might I say, that is just fab,” he said of Lynn's dress. “I'm glad someone noticed,” she replied, seeming to take a stab at me.

examples.text: He had never lost his appreciation for the romantic atmosphere of a studio, and though now the sight of it was like a stab in his heart, without thinking what he was at, he changed slightly the position of a Louis XV. table which was one of his treasures.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 작업실의 낭만적인 분위기에 대한 감상을 결코 잃지 않았고, 지금 그 광경이 가슴을 찌르는 듯했지만, 자신이 무엇을 하고 있는지도 모른 채 그의 보물 중 하나인 루이 15세 양식 탁자의 위치를 살짝 바꾸었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From down + -ward.
definition_en: The direction or movement from top to bottom.

senses.gloss: Toward a lower level, whether in physical space, in a hierarchy, or in amount or value.
senses.example: His position in society moved ever downward.

senses.gloss: At a lower level.
senses.example: Dagon his Name, Sea Monster, upward Man / And downward Fish […]

senses.gloss: Southward.
senses.example: If we turn to the New World, we find that among the American Indians, from the Eskimo of Alaska downward to Brazil and still farther south, homosexual customs have been very frequently observed.

examples.text: his movement caused it to fall, face downwards, on the ground.
examples.translation_ko: 그의 움직임 때문에 캔버스가 앞면이 바닥을 향하게 하여 땅에 떨어졌다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Latin māter (“mother”), partly via Late Middle English matere. Doublet of mata and mother. Ancestor of matrix.
definition_en: A mother

senses.gloss: Mother.
senses.example: “Mater, you look well.” / “I am well. And you,” she said in that dryly prosaic deep voice of hers, “look healed.”

senses.gloss: A meninx; the dura mater, arachnoid mater, or pia mater of the brain.

examples.text: No mater whose the picture, he could not leave it there in the dust, and he raised it; but then curiosity got the better of him.

senses.gloss: To search something thoroughly and with disregard for the way in which things were arranged.

definition_en: Hold or display something, typically a weapon, in a threatening or impressive manner.

senses.gloss: To move or swing a weapon back and forth, particularly if demonstrating anger, threat or skill.

etymology: From Latin tremulus, from tremō (“I tremble, shake”) + -ulus. Doublet of tremor and tremble. By surface analysis, tremulate + -ous.

senses.gloss: Timid, hesitant; lacking confidence.
senses.example: This, hard on the heels of the death of Julia Child in 2004, makes one tremulous about the future.

examples.text: He looked at me with a tremulous smile.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 떨리는 미소를 지으며 나를 바라보았다.

senses.gloss: That which occasions crime.
senses.example: the tree of life, the crime of our first father's fall

senses.gloss: By supernatural or uncommon causes, e.g. by a god; that cannot be explained in terms of normal events.
Very surprising; amazing.

PIE word
 *tréyes

definition_en: Having no value or worth.

examples.translation_ko: 또한 그녀의 과묵함이 무엇인지 모를 것을 감추고 있다고 늘 생각해왔던 것도 기억났다. 하지만 이제 그 속에서 부끄러운 비밀을 숨기려는 욕망 이상의 것을 보았다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From tranquil + -ity, from Middle English tranquillite, from Old French tranquillite, tranquilité, from Latin tranquillitas.
definition_en: A state of being calm and peaceful.

senses.gloss: The state of being tranquil; peacefulness, the absence of disturbance or stress; serenity; calm.

examples.text: Her tranquillity was like the sullen calm that broods over an island which has been swept by a hurricane.
examples.translation_ko: 그녀의 평온함은 허리케인에 휩쓸린 섬 위에 드리워진 음울한 고요와 같았다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English brood, brod, from Old English brōd (“brood; foetus; breeding, hatching”), from Proto-Germanic *brōduz (“heat, breeding”), from ...
definition_en: Think or worry about something repeatedly.

senses.gloss: The young of certain animals, especially a group of young birds or fowl hatched at one time by the same mother.
senses.example: As a hen doth gather her brood under her wings.

senses.gloss: The young of any egg-laying creature, especially if produced at the same time.
The eggs and larvae of social insects such as bees, ants and some wasps, especially when gathered together in special brood chambers or combs within the colony.

examples.text: Her tranquillity was like the sullen calm that broods over an island which has been swept by a hurricane.
examples.translation_ko: 그녀의 평온함은 허리케인에 휩쓸린 섬 위에 드리워진 음울한 고요와 같았다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Cynicism, cynic + -ism; compare cynism.
definition_en: A feeling of distrust or skepticism about the motives of others.

senses.gloss: A distrustful attitude.

An emotion of jaded negativity, or a general distrust of the integrity or professed motives of other people. Cynicism can manifest itself by frustration, disillusionment and distrust in regard to organizations, authorities and other aspects of society, often due to previous bad experience. Cynics often view others as motivated solely by disguised self-interest.
A scornfully pessimistic comment or act.

examples.text: Strickland interrupted my reflections with an observation the profound cynicism of which startled me.
examples.translation_ko: 스트릭랜드가 깊은 냉소주의가 담긴 말로 내 생각을 가로막았는데, 그 말이 나를 놀라게 했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English incurren, from Anglo-Norman encurir, Middle French encourir, from Old French encorre, from Latin incurrere.
definition_en: To suffer or bring upon oneself a penalty, cost, or disadvantage.

senses.gloss: To bring upon oneself or expose oneself to, especially something inconvenient, harmful, or onerous; to become liable or subject to.
senses.example: Cruelty incurs calamity.

senses.gloss: To render (somebody, or oneself) liable or subject to.
senses.example: Lest you incur me much more damage in my fame than you have done me pleasure in preserving my life.

senses.gloss: To enter or pass into.

examples.text: “It must be reassuring to you to know that you certainly run no risk of incurring the resentment of the women you come in contact with,” I retorted.
examples.translation_ko: "당신과 접촉하는 여자들의 원한을 살 위험은 전혀 없다는 걸 아니 안심이 되겠군요." 내가 쏘아붙였다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English principle, from Old French principe, from Latin prīncipium (“beginning, foundation”), from prīnceps (“first”). By surface analy...
definition_en: A fundamental concept or idea that serves as the basis for a theory or system.

senses.gloss: A fundamental assumption or guiding belief.
senses.example: We need some sort of principles to reason from.

senses.gloss: A rule used to choose among solutions to a problem.
senses.example: The principle of least privilege holds that a process should only receive the permissions it needs.

senses.gloss: Moral rule or aspect.
senses.example: I don't doubt your principles.

examples.text: “You are always prepared to sacrifice your principles for a repartee,” he answered.
examples.translation_ko: "당신은 재치 있는 응수를 위해서라면 언제든 자신의 원칙을 희생할 준비가 되어 있군요." 그가 대답했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition_en: Causing puzzlement or confusion.

senses.gloss: present participle and gerund of puzzle

examples.text: Then I came to the question which had seemed to me most puzzling.
examples.translation_ko: 그때 나는 가장 당황스러웠던 문제에 이르렀다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From horror + -ify, or borrowed from Latin horrificare (cf. French horrifier). 1791, in form horrifying.
definition_en: To fill with horror or fear.

senses.gloss: To cause to feel extreme apprehension or unease; to cause to experience horror.
senses.example: The haunted house horrified me, as I passed from one room to the next feeling more and more like I wasn’t going to survive.

examples.text: “At first she was horrified.”
examples.translation_ko: "처음에 그 여자는 소스라치게 놀랐어."
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English wreken, from Old English wrecan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrekan, from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wreg...
definition_en: Cause severe damage or harm.

senses.gloss: To cause harm; to afflict; to inflict; to harm or injure; to let out harm.
senses.example: The earthquake wreaked havoc in the city.

senses.gloss: To chasten, or chastise/chastize, or castigate, or punish, or smite.
senses.example: The police abused their authority to wreak an innocent.

senses.gloss: To inflict or take vengeance on.
senses.example: At heart they hate their horrid fates, and so wreak their poor spite on me who stand for everything they have not, and for all they most crave and never can attain.

examples.text: His life was strangely divorced from material things, and it was as though his body at times wreaked a fearful revenge on his spirit.
examples.translation_ko: 그의 삶은 물질적인 것들과 이상하게 분리되어 있었고, 마치 그의 육체가 때때로 그의 정신에 무서운 복수를 가하는 것 같았다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Latin obsessio (“a besieging”), from obsidere (“to besiege”); see obsess.
definition_en: A persistent and often uncontrolled preoccupation with an idea or activity.

senses.gloss: The quality of being obsessed.
An idea that engenders a compulsive or irrational preoccupation, or the preoccupation thereby engendered.
An activity or entity that inspires a compulsive and potentially unhealthy fixation, or the fixation thereby inspired.
senses.example: Editing Wikipedia started as a hobby, but it's turned into a complete obsession of mine.

examples.text: It was an obsession so complete that there was no room in his soul for prudence or gratitude.
examples.translation_ko: 그것은 너무나 완전한 강박이어서 그의 영혼에는 신중함이나 감사함이 들어설 여지가 없었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English hinderance, hinderaunce, hindraunce, hynderaunce, hynderawnce, hynderawns, hyndrance; equivalent to hinder + -ance.
definition_en: An obstacle or hindrance to progress or success.

senses.gloss: Something which hinders: something that holds back or causes problems with something else.
senses.example: High-heeled shoes may be fashionable, but they can also be a hindrance to walking.

senses.gloss: The state or act of hindering something.
senses.example: Your hindrance of this process will not be tolerated.

examples.text: I can’t overcome my desire, but I hate it; it imprisons my spirit; I look forward to the time when I shall be free from all desire and can give myself without hindrance to my work.
examples.translation_ko: 욕망을 극복할 수는 없지만 증오한다. 욕망이 내 영혼을 가둔다. 모든 욕망에서 해방되어 방해받지 않고 작업에 몰두할 수 있는 때를 고대한다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition_en: A word used to express strong emotions or feelings.

senses.gloss: An exclamation or filled pause; a word or phrase with no particular grammatical relation to a sentence, often an expression of emotion.
senses.example: 322. The parts of speech which are neither declined nor conjugated, are called by the general name of particles. 323. They are adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections.

senses.gloss: An interruption; something interjected

examples.text: But neither here nor elsewhere do I pretend to give his exact words; his vocabulary was small, and he had no gift for framing sentences, so that one had to piece his meaning together out of interjections, the expression of his face, gestures and hackneyed phrases.
examples.translation_ko: 하지만 여기서든 다른 곳에서든 나는 그의 정확한 말을 전한다고 주장하지는 않는다. 그의 어휘는 빈약했고 문장을 구성하는 재능도 없어서, 감탄사와 표정, 몸짓, 그리고 진부한 구절들을 짜맞춰 그의 의미를 파악해야 했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English chatel, from Old French chatel, from Medieval Latin capitāle (English capital), from Latin capitālis (“of the head”), from capu...
definition_en: A person or thing that can be owned.

senses.gloss: Tangible, movable property.
senses.example: […] although of course the firm had changed hands many times over the centuries, […] But the box has always been part of the chattels, as it were.

senses.gloss: A slave.
senses.example: Not all his servants and chattels are wraiths!

examples.text: “You should have lived at a time when women were chattels and men the masters of slaves,” I said.
examples.translation_ko: "당신은 여자가 재산이고 남자가 노예의 주인이던 시대에 태어났어야 했군요." 내가 말했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From coherent + -ly.
definition_en: In a coherent manner.

senses.gloss: In a coherent manner.

examples.text: I could not help laughing at this remark, made in all seriousness; but he went on, walking up and down the room like a caged beast, intent on expressing what he felt, but found such difficulty in putting coherently.
examples.translation_ko: 진지하게 내뱉은 이 말에 웃음을 참을 수 없었지만, 그는 계속해서 우리에 갇힌 짐승처럼 방 안을 오가며 자신이 느끼는 것을 표현하려 애썼다. 하지만 일관성 있게 말로 옮기는 데 큰 어려움을 겪고 있었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English domynacion, from Old French dominacion, from Latin dominātiō (“rule, dominion”), from dominor (“domineer; rule”); see dominate.
definition_en: The state of being dominant or having control over something.

senses.gloss: Control by means of superior ability, influence, position, or resources; prevailing force.
senses.example: First, relations of power and domination have been and continue to be significantly constitutive of social relations in modern societies.

senses.gloss: The exercise of power in ruling; sovereignty; authority; government.
senses.example: In such a [slaveholding] people, the haughtiness of domination combines with the spirit of freedom [...].

senses.gloss: A dominion; an angel from a high order of angels in the celestial hierarchy.
senses.example: Thrones, dominations, princedoms, virtues, powers.

examples.text: Because she’s weak, she has a rage for domination, and nothing less will satisfy her.
examples.translation_ko: 약하기 때문에 지배욕에 사로잡혀 있고, 그것보다 못한 것으로는 만족하지 않는다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English, alteration of uttermest. More at utmost for the etymology of the latter element. Compare in(ner)most.
definition_en: Most extreme or distant point

senses.gloss: Outermost.
Extreme; utmost; of the farthest, greatest, or highest degree.
senses.example: They also that dwell in the uttermost parts are afraid at thy tokens: thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice.

examples.text: The soul of man wanders through the uttermost regions of the universe, and she seeks to imprison it in the circle of her account-book.
examples.translation_ko: 인간의 영혼이 우주의 가장 먼 곳까지 방황하는데, 그녀는 그것을 자신의 가계부 테두리 안에 가두려 한다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English regioun, from Anglo-Norman regiun, from Latin regiō, from regō. Doublet of regio.
definition_en: A particular area or part of a country or the world.

senses.gloss: Any considerable and connected part of a space or surface; specifically, a tract of land or sea of considerable but indefinite extent; a country; a district; in a broad sense, a place without special reference to location or extent but viewed as an entity for geographical, social or cultural reasons.

senses.gloss: Such a division of the city of Rome and of the territory about Rome, of which the number varied at different times; a district, quarter, or ward.
An administrative subdivision of the European Union.

examples.text: The soul of man wanders through the uttermost regions of the universe, and she seeks to imprison it in the circle of her account-book.
examples.translation_ko: 인간의 영혼이 우주의 가장 먼 곳까지 방황하는데, 그녀는 그것을 자신의 가계부 테두리 안에 가두려 한다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From truthful + -ly.
definition_en: Spoken or expressed in a sincere and honest manner.

senses.gloss: In a truthful manner
senses.example: He spoke truthfully.

senses.gloss: Frankly.
senses.example: Truthfully, I didn't suspect a thing.

examples.text: I thought over his question, for I wanted to answer it truthfully, at all events to my soul.
examples.translation_ko: 나는 그의 질문을 곰곰 생각해보았다. 적어도 내 양심에는 진실하게 대답하고 싶었기 때문이다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From un- + balanced.
definition_en: Lacking balance or equilibrium.

senses.gloss: not balanced, without equilibrium
irrational or mentally deranged
expressing support for a certain point of view; biased

examples.text: Blanche Stroeve didn’t commit suicide because I left her, but because she was a foolish and unbalanced woman.
examples.translation_ko: 블랑슈 스트루브가 자살한 것은 내가 그녀를 떠났기 때문이 아니라, 그녀가 어리석고 불안정한 여자였기 때문입니다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

definition_en: Warm and comfortable in a pleasant way.

senses.gloss: Affording comfort and warmth; snug; social and comfortable.
senses.example: One of us must marry well; Meg didn't, Jo won't, Beth can't, yet,—so I shall, and make everything cosy all round.

senses.gloss: Warm and comfortable.
senses.example: I feel very cosy here in my bed.

examples.text: I thought of the happy life that pair had led in the cosy studio in Montmartre, Stroeve and his wife, their simplicity, kindness, and hospitality; it seemed to me cruel that it should have been broken to pieces by a ruthless chance; but the cruellest thing of all was that in fact it made no great difference.
examples.translation_ko: 몽마르트르의 아늑한 화실에서 스트루브와 그의 아내가 보냈던 행복한 나날들, 그들의 순박함과 친절함, 그리고 후한 인정을 생각해보니, 무자비한 우연에 의해 그 모든 것이 산산조각 난 것이 잔혹하게 느껴졌다. 하지만 무엇보다 잔혹한 것은 사실 그것이 별로 중요하지 않다는 점이었다.

examples.translation_ko: 몽마르트르의 아늑한 화실에서 스트루브와 그의 아내가 보냈던 행복한 나날들, 그들의 순박함과 친절함, 그리고 후한 인정을 생각해보니, 무자비한 우연에 의해 그 모든 것이 산산조각 난 것이 잔혹하게 느껴졌다. 하지만 무엇보다 잔혹한 것은 사실 그것이 별로 중요하지 않다는 점이었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English wrecchednesse; equivalent to wretched + -ness.
definition_en: A state of being extremely unhappy or miserable.

senses.gloss: An unhappy state of mental or physical suffering.
senses.example: She saw only that he was quiet and unobtrusive, and she liked him for it. He did not disturb the wretchedness of her mind by ill-timed conversation.

senses.gloss: A state of prolonged misfortune, privation, or anguish.

examples.text: The world went on, and no one was a penny the worse for all that wretchedness.
examples.translation_ko: 세상은 계속 돌아갔고, 그 모든 비참함에도 불구하고 누구 하나 손해 보는 사람은 없었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle French inane, from Latin inānis (“empty, vain, useless”) which is of unknown origin.
definition_en: Lacking sense or meaning; foolish.

senses.gloss: Lacking sense or meaning, often to the point of boredom or annoyance.
senses.example: This supremely gifted kid told me that in the early elementary grades, the songs sung in music class were so inane that he wanted to skip grades already! Eventually he did, so better late than never.

senses.gloss: Purposeless; pointless.
senses.example: Vague and inane instincts.

examples.text: It all seemed useless and inane.
examples.translation_ko: 모든 것이 무의미하고 공허해 보였다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From humoured + -ly.
definition_en: Done with a sense of humor.

senses.gloss: In the specified kind of humour. See good-humouredly, bad-humouredly, ill-humouredly.

examples.text: He chuckled good-humouredly.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 유쾌하게 킬킬 웃었다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From dis- + regard. Compare misregard.
definition_en: Pay no attention to something.

senses.gloss: The act or state of deliberately not paying attention or caring about something.
senses.example: The government's disregard for the needs of disabled people is outrageous.

examples.text: “Is it possible for any man to disregard others entirely?”
examples.translation_ko: "어떤 인간이든 다른 사람들을 완전히 무시하고 살 수 있을까?"
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: Inherited from Middle English humanyte, humanite, humanitye. By surface analysis, human or humane + -ity. Partly displaced mankind, from Old Englis...
definition_en: The quality of being human.

senses.gloss: Humankind; human beings as a group.
senses.example: At last the concourse is relatively clear of humanity and the task of clearing up can begin.

senses.gloss: The human condition or nature.
The quality of being benevolent; humane traits of character; humane qualities or aspects.
senses.example: Think of that; by that sweet girl that old man had a child: hold ye then there can be any utter, hopeless harm in Ahab? No, no, my lad; stricken, blasted, if he be, Ahab has his humanities!

examples.text: Sooner or later the human being in you will yearn for the common bonds of humanity.”
examples.translation_ko: 조만간 당신 안의 인간적인 면이 인간다운 유대를 갈망하게 될 것이다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English fyry, from fyr (“fire”), equivalent to fire + -y.
definition_en: Having or showing a strong and uncontrolled passion.

senses.gloss: Of or relating to fire.
Burning or glowing.
Inflammable or easily ignited.

examples.text: He stood before me, motionless, with a mocking smile in his eyes; but for all that, for a moment I had an inkling of a fiery, tortured spirit, aiming at something greater than could be conceived by anything that was bound up with the flesh.
examples.translation_ko: 그는 내 앞에 움직이지 않고 서서 눈에 조롱하는 미소를 띠고 있었다. 하지만 그럼에도 불구하고 한순간 나는 육체에 얽매인 그 어떤 것으로도 상상할 수 없는 더 위대한 무언가를 추구하는, 불타오르고 고뇌하는 영혼의 기미를 감지했다.
examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham

etymology: From Middle English conceyven, from Old French concevoir, conceveir, from Latin concipiō, concipere (“to devise, to conceive”).
definition_en: Understand or imagine something

senses.gloss: To have a child; to become pregnant (with).
senses.example: Assisted procreation can help those trying to conceive.

senses.gloss: To develop; to form in the mind; to imagine.
senses.example: There are, moreover, grounds for thinking that the Rosaline of Love’s Labour’s Lost was originally conceived of by Shakespeare as pale with black eyes—...

senses.gloss: To imagine (as); to have a conception of; to form a representation of.
senses.example: Can you conceive of him as a leader?

examples.text: He stood before me, motionless, with a mocking smile in his eyes; but for all that, for a moment I had an inkling of a fiery, tortured spirit, aiming at something greater than could be conceived by anything that was bound up with the flesh.

examples.author: W. Somerset Maugham
